commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

content.thinking:
I'm working out how to write this story: a roughly 900-word piece about a lighthouse keeper who collects sea glass, done without tools. The character is a fiction I get to shape, so the pronoun is my call and I'm settling on it now.

I'm drafting the lighthouse story now: a keeper named Ruth who has collected sea glass on the shingle every morning for thirty-one years, the jar on her windowsill, and her late husband Tom teasing her about the hobby. I'm also sketching a plot involving a young relief keeper.

I'm deciding on the next beats: a young relief keeper arrives because the light is being automated, Ruth has to leave, and on her last morning she finds a meaningful piece of glass that she either hands to the newcomer or leaves on the sand for whoever comes after.

I'm weighing the automation news against Ruth's jar: the light will run itself by autumn, and the sea glass she spent decades gathering is about to lose the place it has always belonged to.

I'm settling on Danny as the young relief keeper, a twenty-four-year-old from the mainland who has never seen a lens turn, and I'll write him as "he." On the last morning Ruth walks the shingle with him carrying her crate, and when he asks what she's hoping to find, she tells him she'll know it when she sees it.

I'm still weighing how the story should end: whether Ruth finds one final piece for Danny, or whether the moment is simpler, with the jar itself becoming the gift.

I'm weighing how the ending should land: Ruth stepping down the lighthouse steps for the last time, and whether she leaves a cobalt piece in the sand or in the sill for Danny to find the next morning, something that is his own.

I'm reworking the opening of the lighthouse story: Ruth wound the lens and lit the lamp every night, then walked the shingle each morning looking for sea glass. I'm keeping the glass vivid but worn, the green, white, and amber pieces softened by decades of tide, and tying her patience to the sea's own slow work.

I'm picturing the watch room with the jar on the sill, glass catching the low morning light, and I'm leaning on that image as the story's quiet center. The automation letter arrives in March, and I'm weighing how little the decision cares about what the light has meant to her. Her replacement is Danny, twenty-four and eager, the kind of newcomer who asks about everything.

I'm picking up the scene where Danny walks the shingle with Ruth on her last morning, asking what they're looking for and finding a white piece of glass that she already knows well. We're still searching the tideline, and her search for the one piece she's after is only starting to build toward the ending.

I'm at the moment Ruth finds the cobalt piece and presses it into Danny's hand, telling him to go find his own.

I'm wrapping up the ending: Ruth reaches the top of the cliff path and looks back once, Danny alone on the shingle, bent over a stone. Then she's on the mainland bus that evening with the jar in her lap, imagining the light coming on without her, and she doesn't look back.

I'm reconsidering the closing lines: the story says Ruth turned once at the cliff top, so a flat "she did not look back" would contradict that, and I want the final beat to agree with the earlier moment. I also want Ruth's line to Danny to sound natural, so I'm trying "This one's yours. Go find your own" rather than the clumsier phrasing I had.

I'm going to fix the ending so it doesn't contradict the earlier cliff-top moment: dropping the "did not look back" line and closing on her having the glass, which feels like the right final note.

content.text:
**The Keeper's Jar**

For thirty-one years, Ruth Ashgrove climbed the hundred and twelve iron steps of Halden Point Light each dusk, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and lit the lamp. Each morning, before the mist burned off, she walked the shingle below the cliffs with her head bent, looking for glass.

Not the bright pieces tourists carried home from the coves further south. She wanted the sea's leftovers: bottle green, milk white, amber from ale bottles that had gone down with a schooner and come back a century later. The tide rolled them for decades until their edges softened into something like river stone, frosted as if someone had breathed on them. Nothing she found was sharp anymore. That was the point. The sea had taken its time, and so could she.

Her husband, Tom, had thought the hobby foolish. "You'll be a sea-glass widow by sixty," he'd teased, the summer before the fever took him. She had kept the joke, and the jar.

The jar sat on the sill of the watch room, filled to the shoulder with three decades of finds. In the mornings, when the sun came low across the water, the glass threw small colored lights across the whitewashed wall. She sometimes thought that was the only decoration the lighthouse had ever needed.

In March, a letter arrived from the Northern Lights Authority. The point would be automated by autumn. A photocell and a timer could do what two keepers had done for a hundred and forty years. Ruth argued for a while, then stopped, because the lamp would burn whether she wrote letters or not.

Her replacement was Danny Price, twenty-four, from the mainland, who had never once seen a lens turn. He was earnest and quick and asked about everything: the tide tables, the foghorn's cracked diaphragm, why the third step from the bottom was painted red. She answered what she could. He wrote it all down.

On her last morning, he came down to the shingle with her.

"What are we looking for?" he asked, reaching for the crate she had insisted on carrying herself.

"Whatever the sea decides to give you."

They worked the tideline in silence. Gulls argued overhead. The water was the flat gray of pewter, and the stones clicked under their boots. Danny found a piece of white glass the size of a thumbnail and held it up, delighted, the way a child shows off a shell. Ruth nodded. She had found ten thousand just like it.

For an hour, neither of them found anything of note. Then her foot nudged something in the wrack. She crouched, knees complaining, and brushed the weed aside.

Cobalt. Deep as a summer evening, worn into a smooth lens no bigger than a coin. In thirty-one years she had found only four pieces of blue, and none this clear.

She held it for a long time. She thought of the lamp and the sweep of light that had guided ships past the rocks for a century and a half. The light had never needed any particular keeper. It had only needed someone to climb the steps.

"Here," she said, and pressed the cobalt into Danny's palm.

"I can't take this. You've been looking for these your whole life."

"Thirty-one years," she said. "This one's yours now. Go find your own."

At the top of the cliff path, she turned once. Danny stood alone on the shingle with the morning sun on his back, bending down to look at something in the stones.

That evening, she was on the mainland bus with the jar in her lap, wrapped in a wool scarf. The window was dark, and she could not see Halden Point from here. But she knew the moment the light came on: the first sweep across the water, then the next, steady as a heartbeat, doing its work without her.

She had the glass, and that was enough.
